claim: The corticospinal tract (CST) is generally assumed to convey motor commands to bulbar or spinal motoneurons.
source: It is generally assumed that the main function of the corticospinal tract (CST) is to convey motor commands to bulbar or spinal motoneurons.
evidence: This is stated as a general assumption in the abstract, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: The CST modulates sensory signals at their entry point in the spinal cord through primary afferent depolarization (PAD).
source: Yet the CST has also been shown to modulate sensory signals at their entry point in the spinal cord through primary afferent depolarization (PAD).
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract, drawing from established scientific knowledge.

claim: Motor and sensory modulation commands in mice belong to segregated paths within the CST.
source: By sequentially investigating different routes of corticofugal pathways through electrophysiological recordings and an intersectional viral strategy, we here demonstrate that motor and sensory modulation commands in mice belong to segregated paths within the CST.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from electrophysiological recordings and viral tracing.

claim: Sensory modulation is executed exclusively by the CST via a population of lumbar interneurons located in the deep dorsal horn.
source: Sensory modulation is executed exclusively by the CST via a population of lumbar interneurons located in the deep dorsal horn.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from viral tracing and electrophysiological recordings.

claim: The cortex conveys the motor command via a relay in the upper spinal cord or supraspinal motor centers.
source: In contrast, the cortex conveys the motor command via a relay in the upper spinal cord or supraspinal motor centers.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments and electrophysiological recordings.

claim: At lumbar level, the main role of the CST is the modulation of sensory inputs.
source: At lumbar level, the main role of the CST is thus the modulation of sensory inputs, which is an essential component of the selective tuning of sensory feedback used to ensure well-coordinated and skilled movement.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on experimental data showing sensory modulation but not motor command at the lumbar level.

claim: The primary motor cortex is classically associated with forelimb skilled movements.
source: The primary motor cortex is classically associated to forelimb skilled movements (Starkey et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2015; Miri et al., 2017; Galiñanes et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The primary motor cortex is associated with complex locomotor tasks such as obstacle crossing, leaning scale or beam.
source: The primary motor cortex is classically associated to forelimb skilled movements (Starkey et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2015; Miri et al., 2017; Galiñanes et al., 2018) and to complex locomotor tasks (obstacles crossing, leaning scale or beam, etc.; Beloozerova and Sirota, 1993; DiGiovanna et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2017; Bieler et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The role of the primary motor cortex in rhythmic locomotion appears minor, if anything.
source: while its role in rythmic locomotion appears, if anything, minor (Beloozerova and Sirota, 1993; DiGiovanna et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: A coordinated movement relies on both a proper motor command and online analysis of ongoing multisensory feedback.
source: A coordinated movement relies not only on a proper motor command, but also on the online analysis of an ongoing multisensory feedback indicating whether the movement has reached the planned objective or requires correction (Akay et al., 2014; Fink et al., 2014; Azim and Seki, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specific tuning of peripheral feedback is possible through inhibition of sensory information at different stages of the sensory pathway, known as 'sensory gating'.
source: To optimize the analysis of the overwhelming quantity of reafferent information, specific tuning of peripheral feedback is possible through inhibition of sensory information at different stages of the sensory pathway, a phenomenon known as 'sensory gating' (Seki and Fetz, 2012; McComas, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Sensory gating at the spinal cord level can be mediated by presynaptic inhibition of sensory inputs through primary afferent depolarization (PAD).
source: At the spinal cord level, sensory gating can be mediated by presynaptic inhibition of sensory inputs through primary afferent depolarization (PAD), a powerful mechanism controlled both by supraspinal centers and by adjacent primary afferents (Eccles et al., 1962).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The most studied cause of PAD is presynaptic GABA-A-mediated depolarization.
source: While multiple mechanisms have been demonstrated (Shreckengost et al., 2021), the most studied cause of PAD is presynaptic GABA-A-mediated depolarization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Primary afferents have a high chloride content and respond to GABA by depolarization.
source: Primary afferents have indeed a high chloride content and respond to GABA by a depolarization that has been shown to reduce the amplitude of incoming action potentials and thus inhibit synaptic transmission (Prescott and De Koninck, 2003; Doyon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PAD has been involved in the adjustment of reflex excitability.
source: PAD has been involved in the adjustment of reflex excitability (Rudomin and Schmidt, 1999)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Absence of PAD results in a pathological context associated with spasticity.
source: and its absence results in a pathological context associated with spasticity (Caron et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Proprioceptive feedback is required for skilled locomotion.
source: Proprioceptive feedback is required for skilled locomotion (Akay et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Presynaptic inhibition of sensory feedback is essential for performing smooth forelimb skilled movements in mice.
source: and presynaptic inhibition of sensory feedback is essential for performing smooth forelimb skilled movements in mice (Akay et al., 2014; Fink et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PAD can be evoked by stimulation of the sensorimotor cortex in primates, cat, and rats.
source: Interestingly, PAD can also be evoked by stimulation of the sensorimotor cortex in primates, cat, and rats (Andersen et al., 1962; Carpenter et al., 1963; Andersen et al., 1964; Abdelmoumène et al., 1970; Eguibar et al., 1994; Wall and Lidierth, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Monosynaptic CST-MN contacts are present only in some higher primates.
source: Indeed, monosynaptic CST-MN contacts are present only in some higher primates, while CST-interneuronal connections are preponderant (in adults) across species (rodents and primates) (Alstermark et al., 2011; Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017; Ueno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CST-interneuronal connections are preponderant in adults across species including rodents and primates.
source: Indeed, monosynaptic CST-MN contacts are present only in some higher primates, while CST-interneuronal connections are preponderant (in adults) across species (rodents and primates) (Alstermark et al., 2011; Ebbesen and Brecht, 2017; Ueno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Up to 65% of neurons in genetically distinct spinal populations receive CST inputs.
source: But neurons with identical genetic markers do not necessary share identical function: in these genetically distinct populations, up to 65% of the neurons receive CST inputs (Ueno et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The area inducing DRPs in the mouse sensorimotor cortex was centered at AP = −0.75 mm, L = 1.5 mm.
source: The area inducing the DRPs was centered at AP = −0.75 mm, L = 1.5 mm (Figure 1C, n = 7 mice).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from DRP recordings.

claim: The area inducing EMG in the tibialis anterior was centered at AP = −0.75 mm, L = 1.75 mm.
source: The sensorimotor cortex was similarly mapped with trains of photostimulations (6 × 1 ms pulses, 2 ms apart) and the area inducing EMG was centered at AP = −0.75 mm, L = 1.75 mm (n = 5 mice; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from EMG recordings.

claim: The cortical zones inducing DRPs and EMGs in the hindlimb are concentric.
source: We observed that the two zones are concentric, demonstrating that cortically evoked PAD and motor command of the hindlimb can originate from the same cortical area.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from cortical mapping, as shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 16.4% ± 3.2% of spinal TdTomato-positive neurons (CST targets) were GAD65-GFP+.
source: We evaluated the proportion of GAD65+ neurons among these neurons (Figure 1D,E): 16.4% ± 3.2% of spinal Td-Tomato-positive neurons were GAD65-GFP+ (69 neurons out of 427, n = 3 mice)
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from transynaptic labeling and immunohistochemistry.

claim: Only 2.2% ± 1.8% of CST targets were ChAT-EGFP positive.
source: By performing a similar experiment in ChAT-EGFP mice, we showed that only 2.2% ± 1.8% of CST targets were ChAT-EGFP positive (1 out of 45 neurons, n = 4 mice)
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from transynaptic labeling in ChAT-EGFP mice.

claim: Pyramidotomy completely abolished cortically evoked DRPs.
source: Cortically evoked DRPs were completely abolished by this pyramidotomy (DRP amplitude before: 3.8 µV ± 0.32 µV; after: 0.30 µV ± 0.12 µV, n = 3 mice, p=0.006)
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from DRP recordings before and after pyramidotomy.

claim: Pyramidotomy hardly affected cortically evoked EMGs.
source: whereas cortically evoked EMGs were hardly affected (S/N ratio 3.3 ± 0.61 before, 2.2 ± 0.1 after, n = 4 mice, p=0.517, all Z-scores above significance after lesion, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B; Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from EMG recordings before and after pyramidotomy.

claim: Indirect cortical-to-spinal pathways do not encode cortically evoked DRPs.
source: This demonstrates that indirect cortical-to-spinal pathways (involving supraspinal motor centers) do not encode cortically evoked DRPs but have a major role for cortically evoked motor contraction of the hindlimb.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments showing DRP abolishment but EMG preservation.

claim: Indirect cortical-to-spinal pathways have a major role for cortically evoked motor contraction of the hindlimb.
source: This demonstrates that indirect cortical-to-spinal pathways (involving supraspinal motor centers) do not encode cortically evoked DRPs but have a major role for cortically evoked motor contraction of the hindlimb.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments showing EMG preservation.

claim: In the mouse lumbar cord, the CST mediates cortically evoked DRPs.
source: These results show that, in the mouse lumbar cord, the CST mediates cortically evoked DRPs and hence modulates sensory inputs in a presynaptic manner.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments.

claim: Photostimulation of CS neurons induced a robust EMG signal (S/N ratio 2.4 ± 0.52, n = 5 mice).
source: Photostimulation of CS neurons (at the cortical level) induced a robust EMG signal (S/N ratio 2.4 ± 0.52, n = 5 mice, Figure 3E, upper)
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from EMG recordings after photostimulation of retrogradely labeled CS neurons.

claim: Photostimulation of CS neurons induced DRPs (mean amplitude = 14.5 ± 4.0µV, n = 5).
source: In agreement with the pyramidotomy results (Figure 2C), the photostimulation of CS neurons also induced DRPs (mean amplitude = 14.5 ± 4.0µV, n = 5)
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from DRP recordings after photostimulation of retrogradely labeled CS neurons.

claim: Pyramidotomy completely abolished the EMG signal evoked by cortically activating CS neurons.
source: A pyramidotomy, similar to the ones performed above (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), completely abolished the EMG signal evoked by cortically activating CS neurons (S/N ratio 0.9 ± 0.12; n = 3 mice, p=0.013; all Z-scores below significance after pyramidotomy, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C; Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from EMG recordings before and after pyramidotomy in ChR2-retro mice.

claim: Supraspinal collaterals of the CST do not trigger motor output.
source: This demonstrates that, while supraspinal collaterals of the CST do not trigger motor output, direct spinal branches can drive motor command.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments in ChR2-retro mice.

claim: Direct spinal branches of the CST can drive motor command.
source: This demonstrates that, while supraspinal collaterals of the CST do not trigger motor output, direct spinal branches can drive motor command.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments in ChR2-retro mice.

claim: CST targets were concentrated in spinal lumbar segments L2–L3, rostral to the large pools of motoneurons.
source: We first identified the lumbar segments containing CST targets by using cortical injection of AAV2/1-CBA-WGA-Cre in TdTomato-flex mice (Figure 4A): CST targets were concentrated in spinal lumbar segments L2–L3, rostral to the large pools of motoneurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from transynaptic labeling, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: 85.4% of CST targets were dorsal to the central canal.
source: They were largely located in the dorsal horn (85.4% were dorsal to the central canal), in particular in the contralateral deep dorsal horn (laminae IV to VII) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from transynaptic labeling and histological analysis.

claim: Spinal photostimulation of lumbar CST targets induced DRPs in the ipsilateral lumbar root of eight out of nine mice (2.93 ± 0.48 µV, n = 8 mice).
source: Although the number of ChETA-expressing neurons was highly variable (due to the variability inherent to the WGA-Cre transynaptic tool, see Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and to the intersectional strategy), spinal photostimulation induced DRPs in the ipsilateral lumbar root of eight out of nine mice (2.93 ± 0.48 µV, n = 8 mice, Figure 4E–G)
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from DRP recordings after spinal photostimulation in double-injected mice.

claim: DRPs can be directly controlled by the CST projecting to the lumbar cord through local interneurons.
source: spinal photostimulation induced DRPs in the ipsilateral lumbar root of eight out of nine mice (2.93 ± 0.48 µV, n = 8 mice, Figure 4E–G), demonstrating that DRPs can be directly controlled by the CST projecting to the lumbar cord through local interneurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from DRP recordings after spinal photostimulation in double-injected mice.

claim: The amplitude of DRPs was not related to the number of ChETA-expressing spinal neurons.
source: Interestingly, the amplitude of the DRPs was not related to the number of ChETA-expressing spinal neurons, suggesting that probably only a fraction of those are involved in primary afferent control.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data analysis, as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Photostimulation of lumbar targets of the CST failed to elicit hindlimb movements or muscle contraction.
source: However, photostimulation of these same lumbar targets of the CST (same animals) failed to elicit hindlimb movements or muscle contraction as attested by EMG recordings (S/N ratio 1.0 ± 0.02; n = 7 mice, Z-scores below significance, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D; Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is a primary finding based on experimental data from EMG recordings after spinal photostimulation in double-injected mice.

claim: CS neurons are able to evoke motor contraction by activation of their spinal targets, but these targets are not located in the lumbar cord but rather at another spinal level.
source: Together with the results presented in Figure 3, we can conclude that CS neurons are able to evoke motor contraction by activation of their spinal targets, but that these targets are not located in the lumbar cord but rather at another spinal level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from multiple experiments showing EMG responses from cortical but not lumbar stimulation of CST targets.

claim: Cortically evoked DRPs and EMGs follow a similar corticofugal pathway that segregates at the spinal level.
source: Cortically evoked DRPs and EMGs thus follow a similar corticofugal pathway that segregates at the spinal level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from multiple experiments showing different spinal pathways for DRPs and EMGs.

claim: A large fraction of the cortical motor command to the hindlimb is conveyed through non-CST pathways.
source: Our study concludes that a large fraction of the cortical motor command to the hindlimb is conveyed through non-CST pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments showing preserved EMG responses.

claim: Non-CST pathways conveying motor command could involve the reticular formation or the red nucleus.
source: These could involve the reticular formation or the red nucleus that receive cortical innervation, project directly or indirectly onto spinal motoneurons, and control different parameters of movements (Lavoie and Drew, 2002; Zelenin et al., 2010; Esposito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation based on known anatomy and citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortically evoked PAD is exclusively relayed through the CST.
source: Beyond inducing hindlimb muscle contraction, we have characterized the ability of the cortex to induce DRPs, which is a measure of PAD (Wall and Lidierth, 1997). We demonstrate that it is exclusively relayed through the CST
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments showing complete abolishment of DRPs.

claim: The targets of the CST are predominantly located in laminae IV–VI.
source: The targets of the CST identified by our transynaptic labeling are indeed predominantly located in laminae IV–VI and include a small population of GAD65-expressing neurons.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data from transynaptic labeling and histological analysis.

claim: Stimulation of the red nucleus and the reticular formation is known to induce PAD.
source: In addition to the sensorimotor cortex, stimulation of other supraspinal nuclei is known to induce PAD. This is the case of the red nucleus and the reticular formation (Jiménez et al., 1987; Sirois et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The ability of the red nucleus and reticular formation to induce PAD does not rely on a sensorimotor cortical command.
source: The corticorubral and corticoreticular tracts were preserved by the pyramidotomy, yet the cortically induced PAD was completely lost. This strongly suggests that the ability of the red nucleus and reticular formation to induce PAD does not rely on a sensorimotor cortical command.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments.

claim: GAD65-expressing neurons are essential for smoothed forelimb movements.
source: GAD65-expressing neurons are essential for smoothed forelimb movements (Fink et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Sensory information is inhibited in a modality- and phase-dependent manner during forelimb voluntary movements in primates.
source: Similarly, recordings in primates demonstrated that sensory information is inhibited in a modality- and phase-dependent manner during forelimb voluntary movements (Seki et al., 2003; Seki et al., 2009; Seki and Fetz, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The change in afferent fiber excitability accompanying sensory presynaptic inhibition in primates was smaller than 2 µV.
source: Importantly, the change in afferent fiber excitability (Wall, 1958) accompanying the sensory presynaptic inhibition in primates was even smaller (<2 µV; Seki et al., 2003) than the DRPs we report as a consequence of cortical stimulation
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cortically evoked DRPs might be sufficient to significantly impact the transmission of sensory information.
source: Importantly, the change in afferent fiber excitability (Wall, 1958) accompanying the sensory presynaptic inhibition in primates was even smaller (<2 µV; Seki et al., 2003) than the DRPs we report as a consequence of cortical stimulation, suggesting that cortically evoked DRPs might be sufficient to significantly impact the transmission of sensory information.
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: CS neurons from the same sensorimotor cortex area are able to relay both motor command and sensory modulation to hindlimb, but through segregated pathways.
source: Here, we demonstrate that CS neurons from the same sensorimotor cortex area (but not necessarily a single population) are able to relay both motor command and sensory modulation to hindlimb, but through segregated pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from multiple experiments.

claim: Specific stimulation of the CST at the cervical level induces forelimb contraction.
source: In contrast with the present results on hindlimbs, specific stimulation of the CST at the cervical level induces forelimb contraction (Gu et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mice do not display an extensive repertoire of skilled hindlimb movements relative to the forelimb.
source: Relative to the forelimb, mice do not display an extensive repertoire of skilled hindlimb movements and a difference in the level of cortical control is expected.
evidence: This is based on general knowledge about mouse motor behavior.

claim: The CST travels mainly in the dorsal funiculus in rodents.
source: From an anatomical point of view, this tract travels mainly in the dorsal funiculus in rodents, while it is located in the dorsolateral funiculus in primates, and its projection area within the spinal cord accordingly differs (Lemon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The CST is located in the dorsolateral funiculus in primates.
source: From an anatomical point of view, this tract travels mainly in the dorsal funiculus in rodents, while it is located in the dorsolateral funiculus in primates, and its projection area within the spinal cord accordingly differs (Lemon, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The evolution of the CST has been linked to the development of the most dexterous movements that can be performed by primates.
source: The evolution of the CST has been linked to the development of the most dexterous movements that can be performed by primates, with the appearance of direct cortico-motoneuronal (CMN) contacts that are absent in rodents.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Direct cortico-motoneuronal (CMN) contacts are absent in rodents.
source: The evolution of the CST has been linked to the development of the most dexterous movements that can be performed by primates, with the appearance of direct cortico-motoneuronal (CMN) contacts that are absent in rodents.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Primate CS neurons abundantly project onto spinal interneurons in addition to forming CMN contacts.
source: Importantly, primate CS neurons do not only form CMN contacts but also abundantly project onto spinal interneurons, and the sensory control function of the CST we report has also been proposed in primates (Lemon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The sensory control function of the CST has been proposed in primates.
source: Importantly, primate CS neurons do not only form CMN contacts but also abundantly project onto spinal interneurons, and the sensory control function of the CST we report has also been proposed in primates (Lemon, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The direct CST is able to induce motor contraction, independently of its supraspinal collaterals, through spinal targets possibly located at the cervico-thoracic level.
source: Altogether, our results support a segregation of pathways involved in cortically evoked sensory modulation vs. motor control. The direct CST is able to induce motor contraction, independently of its supraspinal collaterals, through spinal targets possibly located at the cervico-thoracic level.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from multiple experiments.

claim: Motor command is largely mediated by non-CST pathways, most likely cortico-rubral, or -reticular ones.
source: However, we show that motor command is largely mediated by non-CST pathways, most likely cortico-rubral, or -reticular ones.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from pyramidotomy experiments.

claim: The major and essential role of the lumbar rodent CST is hindlimb sensory modulation at the primary afferent level through a population of lumbar target neurons.
source: On the other hand, the major and essential role of the lumbar rodent CST appears to be hindlimb sensory modulation at the primary afferent level through a population of lumbar target neurons whose activation is sufficient to produce DRPs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from multiple experiments.

claim: Photostimulation of the sensorimotor cortex in mice expressing only EGFP in CS neurons leads to no DRP signal.
source: Similar photostimulation of this area in mice expressing only the fluorescent reporter EGFP in corticospinal (CS) neurons leads to no DRP signal (see below and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a control experiment result referenced in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Photostimulation of the sensorimotor cortex in mice expressing only EGFP in CS neurons leads to no EMG signal.
source: Again, similar photostimulation of this area in mice expressing only EGFP in CS neurons leads to no EMG signal (see below and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a control experiment result referenced in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: GABAergic terminals presynaptic to proprioceptive fibers arise from GAD65 interneurons.
source: GABAergic terminals presynaptic to proprioceptive fibers arise from GAD65 interneurons (Hughes et al., 2005; Betley et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Activation of GAD65 interneurons produces DRPs.
source: and their activation produces DRPs (Fink et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cholinergic neurons in the spinal dorsal horn are a subpopulation of GABAergic neurons.
source: In the spinal dorsal horn, cholinergic neurons are a subpopulation of GABAergic neurons (Todd, 1991; Mesnage et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cholinergic terminals are presynaptic to primary afferents.
source: and cholinergic terminals are known to be presynaptic to primary afferents (Ribeiro-da-Silva and Cuello, 1990; Pawlowski et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cholinergic terminals modulate primary afferent inputs.
source: and have recently been shown to modulate primary afferent inputs (Hochman et al., 2010; Shreckengost et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: WGA provides exclusively anterograde transneuronal tracing when expressed in transgenic mice.
source: In contrast to its retrograde and anterograde transport when directly injected (LeVay and Voigt, 1990), WGA is reported to provide an exclusively anterograde transneuronal tracing when expressed in transgenic mice (Braz et al., 2002) or virally, including in the form of a WGA-Cre fusion (Gradinaru et al., 2010; Libbrecht et al., 2017), but see Xu and Südhof, 2013.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies, with a caveat noted.

claim: The absence of direct spino-cortical projection ensures that spinal Td-Tomato-expressing neurons are direct targets of the CST.
source: While a retrograde transynaptic labeling is difficult to exclude in the brain due to the reciprocal connections of the cortex with its targets, the absence of direct spino-cortical projection (and absence of labeling in the ascending tracts, see Figure 1—figure supplement 2E) ensures that spinal Td-Tomato-expressing neurons are direct targets of the CST.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on anatomical knowledge and experimental observations.

claim: CS neurons projecting to the lumbar spinal cord can give off collaterals at the cervico-thoracic level.
source: Because both DRPs and EMGs of a given limb are encoded by the same sensorimotor cortical area and can be conveyed by the spinal branch of the CST, we next interrogated whether these functions are segregated at the spinal level. CS neurons projecting to the lumbar spinal cord can give off collaterals at the cervico-thoracic level (Kamiyama et al., 2015; Karadimas et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CS neurons contact cervical propriospinal neurons.
source: CS neurons projecting to the lumbar spinal cord can give off collaterals at the cervico-thoracic level (Kamiyama et al., 2015; Karadimas et al., 2020) and contact cervical propriospinal neurons (Ueno et al., 2012; Ni et al., 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Cervical propriospinal neurons project to lumbar motoneurons to relay motor command.
source: and contact cervical propriospinal neurons (Ueno et al., 2012; Ni et al., 2014) that in turn project to lumbar motoneurons to relay motor command (Ni et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Cervical propriospinal neurons are involved in segmental coordination.
source: Indeed, many experiments demonstrated that these neurons are involved in segmental coordination (Miller et al., 1975; Nathan et al., 1996; Reed et al., 2006; Reed et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The number of CST targets was not correlated with the delay between the infection and the histological analysis.
source: Consistently with the monosynaptic nature of the transynaptic labeling, their number was not correlated with the delay between the infection and the histological analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Surface photostimulation of the spinal cord in Thy1-ChR2 animals produced an EMG signal.
source: As surface photostimulation of the spinal cord in Thy1-ChR2 animals produced an EMG signal and directly activated neurons even in the deep dorsal horn (Figure 4—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Spinal photostimulation in animals expressing ChETA in CST targets induced a spinal LFP observable as deep as 1150 µm from the surface.
source: This stimulation induced a spinal LFP observable as deep as 1150 µm from the surface (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The cortical area inducing hindlimb contraction in mice is similar to that previously reported.
source: In our study, the cortical area inducing hindlimb contraction is similar to that previously reported in mice (Li and Waters, 1991; Ayling et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cortical area inducing hindlimb contraction spans over the motor cortex and partly over the primary somatosensory cortex.
source: This cortical area (centered around 1 mm caudal and 1.5 mm lateral to Bregma) spans over the motor cortex and also partly over the primary somatosensory cortex according to some atlases and studies (Kirkcaldie et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2018; Karadimas et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and atlases.

claim: CS neurons from the forelimb areas are spatially segregated, forming clusters projecting either to the dorsal or to the intermediate-ventral cervical cord.
source: Indeed, the CS neurons from the forelimb areas are spatially segregated (forming clusters projecting either to the dorsal or to the intermediate-ventral cervical cord), while those from the HLA are largely intermingled (Olivares-Moreno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: CS neurons from the hindlimb area (HLA) are largely intermingled.
source: Indeed, the CS neurons from the forelimb areas are spatially segregated (forming clusters projecting either to the dorsal or to the intermediate-ventral cervical cord), while those from the HLA are largely intermingled (Olivares-Moreno et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The reticular formation and red nucleus receive cortical innervation and project directly or indirectly onto spinal motoneurons.
source: These could involve the reticular formation or the red nucleus that receive cortical innervation, project directly or indirectly onto spinal motoneurons, and control different parameters of movements (Lavoie and Drew, 2002; Zelenin et al., 2010; Esposito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The reticular formation and red nucleus control different parameters of movements.
source: These could involve the reticular formation or the red nucleus that receive cortical innervation, project directly or indirectly onto spinal motoneurons, and control different parameters of movements (Lavoie and Drew, 2002; Zelenin et al., 2010; Esposito et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The most studied mechanism of segmental PAD involves a presynaptic GABAergic last order neuron located in laminae V–VI.
source: The most studied mechanism of segmental PAD involves a presynaptic GABAergic last order neuron (mostly expressing GAD65; Betley et al., 2009), located in laminae V–VI, under the control of a first-order excitatory interneuron that receives peripheral and descending (including cortical) inputs (Eccles et al., 1962; Rudomin and Schmidt, 1999; Betley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The GABAergic last order neuron mediating PAD is under the control of a first-order excitatory interneuron that receives peripheral and descending inputs.
source: The most studied mechanism of segmental PAD involves a presynaptic GABAergic last order neuron (mostly expressing GAD65; Betley et al., 2009), located in laminae V–VI, under the control of a first-order excitatory interneuron that receives peripheral and descending (including cortical) inputs (Eccles et al., 1962; Rudomin and Schmidt, 1999; Betley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Many CS neurons have collaterals at different spinal segments.
source: Although we selectively study CS projecting at least to the lumbar cord (through lumbar retrograde infection), many CS neurons have collaterals at different spinal segments (Kamiyama et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: Photostimulation of CS neurons at the sensorimotor cortex level would activate cervical pathways in addition to lumbar ones.
source: Therefore, their photostimulation at the sensorimotor cortex level would activate cervical pathways in addition to lumbar ones.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the anatomical knowledge that CS neurons have collaterals at different spinal segments.

claim: Cortically evoked PAD in cats is abolished by pyramidotomy.
source: The CST has also been involved in cortically evoked PAD in cats as a pyramidotomy abolishes it (Rudomin et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: The pyramidotomy performed in this study spared CST collaterals targeting brainstem motor nuclei.
source: In this study, we have consistently performed a caudal pyramidotomy, sparing CST collaterals targeting brainstem motor nuclei that branch more rostrally (Akintunde and Buxton, 1992; Alstermark and Pettersson, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies describing the anatomy of CST collaterals.

claim: The pyramidotomy performed in this study spared rubrospinal or reticulospinal tracts.
source: as well as rubrospinal or reticulospinal tracts that can be activated by corticorubral or corticoreticular neurons (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is based on the anatomical location of the lesion and known anatomy of these tracts.

claim: Intraspinal AAV injection did not lead to retrograde infection of CS neurons.
source: There was no ChETA-EYFP labeling in the dorsal funiculus, demonstrating that the intraspinal AAV injection did not lead to retrograde infection of CS neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Intraspinal injections did not affect the general behavior of mice.
source: Intraspinal injections did not affect the general behavior of mice (e.g., no visible motor deficits nor pain-like behaviors) nor induced long-lasting weight loss.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedures.

claim: Surface photostimulation can directly activate neurons located up to 700 µm from the surface.
source: We also demonstrate direct photoactivation of neurons located up to 700 µm from the surface with the short 1 ms stimulus used for EMG recordings.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: 73% of the targets of the CST are located within 700 µm from the surface.
source: As 73% of the targets of the CST are located within 700 µm from the surface, this demonstrates that the large majority of this population can be directly activated by this procedure.
evidence: This is a finding based on experimental data analysis.

claim: Caggiano and colleagues were able to induce motor contraction in ChAT-ChR2 animals using surface photostimulation.
source: Finally, using a similar surface photostimulation with powers equal to or lower than in the present study, Caggiano and colleagues were able to induce motor contraction in ChAT-ChR2 animals and interpreted this as direct activation of motoneurons located in the deep ventral horn (Caggiano et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.
